Chapter 12: The Lantern Market

Previous Chapter Table of Contents Next Chapter

Translator: Quill   Editor: Marrow

The lanterns of the night market were already burning when Ilsa reached the bottom of the hill. Paper globes in red and amber swung from wires strung between the roofs, and every gust off the river set them nodding like a crowd of sleepy heads.

She kept her hood low. The heron pin was wrapped in a handkerchief and pushed deep into her boot, where it pressed a cold oval against her ankle with every step she took over the wet cobbles.

“You’re late,” said Tobin, stepping out from behind a stall that sold candied ginger. He had a smear of soot across one cheek and the restless look of a boy who had been waiting far too long in one place.

“I was followed,” Ilsa said. “Two of them. I lost them near the dye works, I think.”

“You think?”

She did not answer. Instead she watched the crowd, counting the faces she knew and the ones she did not. A fishmonger was arguing with a customer about the price of eels. Three apprentices from the glass guild were laughing over a shared bowl of noodles. Nobody seemed to look at her twice.

* * *

The fortune teller’s tent stood at the far end of the market, wedged between a cobbler and a man who sharpened knives on a foot-powered wheel. Its canvas had once been blue, but years of rain had faded it to the color of an old bruise.

Inside, the air smelled of cloves and lamp oil. An old woman sat behind a low table covered with a cloth embroidered in silver thread, and she did not look up when they entered.

“Sit,” she said. “Both of you. The boy may stand if he prefers, but he will regret it.”

Tobin sat.

Ilsa knelt and drew the handkerchief from her boot. When she unfolded it, the pin caught the lamplight and threw a thin blade of brightness across the old woman’s hands. For a moment nobody breathed.

“So,” the fortune teller murmured at last. “The heron has come home to roost. I wondered whether I would live long enough to see it.”

Outside, somewhere beyond the canvas, a lantern wire snapped, and the whole market seemed to hold its breath with them.
